title: Jason Lewis's human-powered circumnavigation
why_famous: Lewis completed a Guinness-recognized human-powered circumnavigation after thirteen years, using pedal boat, bicycle, skates, kayak, and other human-powered travel.
route_summary: Greenwich–Portugal–Atlantic–North America–Pacific–Australia–Southeast Asia–India–Arabian Sea–Africa–Europe–Greenwich.
source_title: Jason Lewis — global circumnavigation
geometry_note: Continental legs show broad published corridors, not a continuous GPS track. Ocean legs use named landfalls and open-water waypoints; mode changes are separated. The Egypt–Jordan land-border route follows Lewis's own July 2007 journal.

anchors.note: Lewis reports cycling north along the Red Sea coast

title: Erden Eruç's solo human-powered circumnavigation
why_famous: Eruç completed the first solo human-powered circumnavigation, rowing three oceans and crossing land by bicycle, foot, and kayak.
route_summary: Bodega Bay–Papua New Guinea–Australia–Madagascar–Africa–Venezuela–Louisiana–Bodega Bay.
source_title: Around-n-Over — circumnavigation summary
geometry_note: Published stage endpoints are preserved. Intermediate ocean points illustrate broad corridors, not a recorded track; land segments simplify roads and trails.

title: Nansen's Greenland ice-sheet crossing
why_famous: Nansen and five companions, including Sámi skiers Samuel Balto and Ole Ravna, made the first crossing of Greenland's ice sheet.
route_summary: Umivik on the east coast across the ice sheet to the Ameralik Fjord and Nuuk area.
source_title: Fram Museum — Across the Greenland Ice
geometry_note: East and west landing regions are known, but intermediate ice-sheet points represent a broad corridor rather than camp coordinates.

title: Scott's South Pole journey
why_famous: Scott's party reached the South Pole after Amundsen and all five men died on the return journey, making it one of the best-known polar tragedies.
route_summary: Cape Evans–Ross Ice Shelf–Beardmore Glacier–South Pole–return toward One Ton Depot.
source_title: Royal Museums Greenwich — race to the South Pole
geometry_note: Camp and glacier waypoints are approximate. The return is a separate leg ending near the last camp rather than falsely completing a loop. The South Pole has no unique longitude; 160°E is used here for map continuity.

title: Hillary and Tenzing's first Everest summit
why_famous: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay achieved the first confirmed ascent of Mount Everest.
route_summary: South Base Camp–Khumbu Icefall–Western Cwm–Lhotse Face–South Col–southeast ridge–summit.
source_title: Royal Geographical Society — Everest 1953
geometry_note: Known route features are shown schematically; geographic line spacing cannot represent cliffs, crevasses, or vertical exposure.

title: Messner and Habeler's oxygen-free Everest ascent
why_famous: Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler became the first climbers to summit Everest without supplemental oxygen.
route_summary: Nepal side via the South Col and southeast ridge to Everest summit.
source_title: American Alpine Club — 1978 Everest account
geometry_note: Route-feature anchors are schematic and do not show the exact line of the climb or exposure.

title: Messner's solo Everest ascent
why_famous: Messner made the first solo Everest ascent without supplemental oxygen, using the north side of the mountain.
route_summary: North Base Camp–East Rongbuk area–North Col–north face/Great Couloir–Everest summit.
source_title: American Alpine Club — Everest route register
geometry_note: North-face route features are approximate; a flat map cannot represent the steep Great Couloir or exact climbing line.

title: Earl Shaffer's Appalachian Trail thru-hike
why_famous: Shaffer completed the first reported end-to-end Appalachian Trail thru-hike in a single season.
route_summary: Springer Mountain, Georgia, to Mount Katahdin, Maine, by the Appalachian Trail.
source_title: Appalachian Trail Conservancy — The Long Cruise
geometry_note: Named trail regions reconstruct the trail corridor; the exact 1948 alignment changed in many places afterward.

title: Grandma Gatewood's Appalachian Trail hike
why_famous: Emma Gatewood became the first woman to complete the Appalachian Trail alone, challenging ideas about who belonged outdoors.
route_summary: Springer Mountain to Mount Katahdin along the Appalachian Trail.
source_title: Appalachian Trail Conservancy — Trail Tested
geometry_note: Trail-region anchors show the general 1955 corridor, not Gatewood's observed path or the exact historic trail alignment.

title: Cheryl Strayed's Pacific Crest Trail journey
why_famous: The solo walk became the subject of the memoir Wild and introduced many readers to long-distance hiking.
route_summary: Tehachapi Pass through California and Oregon to Bridge of the Gods, the section she actually hiked.
source_title: Pacific Crest Trail Association — Hikes from Wild
geometry_note: PCTA confirms selected locations. Connecting lines approximate the walking corridor and should not imply every intervening mile was walked.

title: Ed Stafford walks the Amazon
why_famous: Stafford made the first recorded walk along the full length of the Amazon River system.
route_summary: Nevado Mismi in Peru along Amazon headwater and river corridors to the Atlantic mouth in Brazil.
source_title: Guinness World Records — walk the Amazon
geometry_note: The route was an overland walk near the river, not a passage along the water centerline. Settlement anchors are broad and do not recover daily detours or bank choices.

title: Mark Beaumont's 78-day world cycle
why_famous: Beaumont completed an officially recognized bicycle circumnavigation in 78 days, setting a new speed mark.
route_summary: Paris–Beijing; Perth–Brisbane; Invercargill–Auckland; Anchorage–Halifax; Lisbon–Paris, with flights omitted.
source_title: Guinness World Records — Mark Beaumont
geometry_note: Major stages are confirmed; inland waypoints approximate roads. Transoceanic flights remain gaps.

title: Jenny Graham's unsupported world cycle
why_famous: Graham set a women's unsupported bicycle circumnavigation speed record in 2018, riding solo across four major cycling stages.
route_summary: Berlin–Beijing; Perth–Brisbane; Invercargill–Auckland; Anchorage–Halifax; Lisbon–Berlin, with flights omitted.
source_title: Jenny Graham — round the world itinerary
geometry_note: Graham's own stage list fixes the endpoints and regions. Inland roads are schematic; flights remain gaps.

title: Annie Londonderry's bicycle world journey
why_famous: Her highly publicized journey made Annie Londonderry a pioneering figure in women's cycling and self-promotion.
route_summary: Boston–Chicago–New York; European and Asian bicycle stages; San Francisco–Boston, with ship travel between continents.
source_title: Smithsonian Magazine — Annie Londonderry
geometry_note: The historical itinerary used ships as well as bicycles. Only broad bicycle legs are shown; precise roads and some stop order require further archival confirmation.

title: Thomas Stevens's bicycle journey around the world
why_famous: Stevens became the first person to travel around the world with a bicycle, combining riding with sea crossings.
route_summary: San Francisco–Boston; Europe–Tehran; Karachi–Kolkata; Chinese and Japanese rides, with ship and other transport gaps.
source_title: International Conference on the History of Cartography — Stevens route study
geometry_note: The bicycle voyage used steamers and other transport. Each mapped ride is separate; historic road alignments are schematic.

title: 25th Infantry Bicycle Corps ride
why_famous: Black U.S. soldiers rode roughly 1,900 miles from Montana to Missouri in a major military test of bicycle transport.
route_summary: Fort Missoula–Yellowstone region–Wyoming–Nebraska–Kansas–St. Louis.
source_title: U.S. Army Transportation Corps — Iron Riders
geometry_note: Military itinerary and settlements define the corridor; individual 1897 tracks and road surfaces are not fully recovered.

title: Oskar Speck kayaks from Germany to Australia
why_famous: Speck paddled a folding kayak from Germany through the Middle East and Asia to Australia over seven years.
route_summary: Ulm–Danube; Euphrates–Persian Gulf; South Asian coasts–Strait of Malacca–Indonesia–Papua New Guinea–Saibai Island.
source_title: Australian National Maritime Museum collection
geometry_note: Museum's country list and known rivers guide broad coastal corridors. The route from the Danube to Syria is a gap; intermediate waterways and port choices need archival verification. Sea waypoints are illustrative and do not recover Speck's actual daily course.

title: Paul Caffyn kayaks around Australia
why_famous: Caffyn completed the first sea-kayak circumnavigation of mainland Australia, a year-long voyage of roughly 15,000 km.
route_summary: Queenscliff–east coast–Gulf of Carpentaria–Darwin–Kimberley–west coast–Great Australian Bight–Queenscliff.
source_title: Expedition Kayak — Caffyn Australia
geometry_note: Coastal capes and towns outline the voyage, not daily landings. Northern Gulf waypoints follow the shore rather than drawing a shortcut across land.

title: Freya Hoffmeister kayaks around Australia
why_famous: Hoffmeister became the first woman to sea-kayak around mainland Australia, completing an anticlockwise circuit.
route_summary: Queenscliff–east coast–Cape York–Gulf of Carpentaria crossing–Broome–west coast–southern coast–Queenscliff.
source_title: Freya Hoffmeister — Australia expedition
geometry_note: Major coastal points come from the expedition record. The Gulf of Carpentaria crossing is shown offshore; other stretches are simplified coastal corridors.

title: Aleksander Doba kayaks across the Atlantic
why_famous: Doba made a solo human-propelled kayak crossing from Europe to mainland North America, stopping at Bermuda.
route_summary: Lisbon–Bermuda–Cape Canaveral, Florida.
source_title: Guinness World Records — Doba Atlantic kayak
geometry_note: Lisbon, Bermuda, and Canaveral are documented; intermediate ocean waypoints are illustrative and not GPS fixes.

title: John Fairfax's solo Atlantic row
why_famous: Fairfax became the first person to row any ocean solo, crossing the Atlantic from the Canaries to Florida.
route_summary: San Agustín, Gran Canaria, to Hollywood Beach near Miami.
source_title: Guinness World Records — first solo ocean row
geometry_note: Departure and landfall are documented; ocean waypoints sketch a possible corridor and are not observed positions.

title: Tori Murden's solo Atlantic row
why_famous: Murden became the first woman to row an ocean solo, reaching Guadeloupe after departing Tenerife.
route_summary: Tenerife, Canary Islands, to Guadeloupe.
source_title: Guinness World Records — first solo ocean row by a woman
geometry_note: Endpoints are documented; ocean waypoints are illustrative, not a reconstruction of wind-driven drift.

title: Roz Savage's solo Pacific row
why_famous: Savage became the first woman to row the Pacific solo, completing it in three stages.
route_summary: San Francisco–Hawaii–Tarawa, Kiribati–Papua New Guinea.
source_title: Guinness World Records — Savage Pacific row
geometry_note: Stage endpoints are supported by the record source; open-water points are illustrative and each stage is separate.

title: Sarah Outen's North Pacific row
why_famous: Outen became the first woman to row the Pacific west to east solo; hazardous conditions required a tow for final harbor entry.
route_summary: Choshi, Japan, to waters off Adak, Alaska; assisted tow to harbor is not shown as rowing.
source_title: Guinness World Records — Sarah Outen Pacific row
geometry_note: The source gives the exact end-of-row coordinate off Adak. Other ocean waypoints are illustrative; the final tow is a distinct segment.

title: Felicity Aston's solo Antarctic crossing
why_famous: Aston became the first woman to ski solo across Antarctica, covering 1,744 km from the Ross side through the South Pole to Hercules Inlet.
route_summary: Ross Ice Shelf–Leverett Glacier–South Pole–Hercules Inlet.
source_title: Guinness World Records — Aston Antarctic crossing
geometry_note: The glacier, pole, and finish are known route features, but plateau waypoints are schematic. Expedition was resupplied and used a flagged route. The South Pole has no unique longitude; 90°W is used here for map continuity.
